strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether non-uniform generation is equivalent to non-uniform noise-dependent generation (answered negatively, with a strong separation at noise level 1), and (2) a characterization for non-uniform noise-dependent generatability (Theorem 4.7).

The central technical result (Theorem 2.14) — that generation with any finite noise level i ≥ 1 is equivalent to generation with noise level 1, for both uniform and non-uniform notions — is genuinely surprising given the strict noise-level hierarchy shown for generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026). This nontrivial contrast is a meaningful conceptual contribution.

The core technical lemma (Lemma 3.2), which shows NC_{i-1}(C) ≥ floor(sqrt(NC_i(C))), is a clever combinatorial argument (partitioning and pigeonhole over noisy closures) that cleanly drives the main equivalence result.

The separation construction in Theorem 2.15 (disjoint 'column' languages) is a careful and non-trivial adversarial argument covering multiple exhaustive cases, and it yields a strong result (separation with just a single noisy string).

The resulting characterizations (Theorems 2.16 and 2.17) are notably simpler than prior characterizations from RR25 (reducing an infinite family of conditions NC_i(C) < ∞ for all i to a single condition NC_1(C) < ∞), which is a nice simplification with explanatory value.
weaknesses: The paper is a highly specialized theoretical contribution within a narrow and fast-growing subfield (formal language generation in the limit), evidenced by the large number of very recent, closely related arXiv/conference papers (2025–2026) cited and built upon. Its significance to the broader ICML audience and to practical understanding of LLM behavior is unclear; the connection between 'noisy enumeration' abstractions and real-world noisy training data is asserted in the introduction but never substantiated or discussed further.

There is no empirical or illustrative validation, and more importantly no discussion connecting the abstract combinatorial results back to any practical implications for actual language generation systems, despite motivating language about noisy training data and LLM hallucination in the introduction.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, assuming substantial familiarity with a chain of prior papers (KM24, LRT25, RR25, BPZ26) with minimal self-contained intuition; e.g., Lemma 3.2's proof strategy and Theorem 2.15's exhaustive case analysis are not given intuitive high-level summaries before diving into the formal argument, which limits accessibility.

No explicit limitations section or discussion of the practical scope/boundaries of the noisy-generation model (e.g., is the strict noise-level assumption, unique-string requirement, or countability of the universe restrictive in practice?).

The significance of resolving open questions is somewhat self-referential to a narrow set of very recent papers (mostly 2025/2026, several still in proceedings or on arXiv), so the broader impact and staying power of the specific open questions being resolved is unclear at this early stage of the subfield's development.

strengths: The paper addresses well-defined open questions explicitly posed in Raman and Raman (2025) concerning the relationship between non-uniform generation and non-uniform noise-dependent generation, and provides a complete characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability that was previously unknown.

The technical results are non-trivial and somewhat surprising: showing that generation with noise level 1 is equivalent to generation with any finite noise level i≥1, in sharp contrast to the strict hierarchy established for noisy generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026). This juxtaposition is an interesting structural finding about the uniform/non-uniform noisy setting.

The constructions supporting the separation result (Theorem 2.15) are intricate and the authors handle multiple adversarial cases carefully (the three-way case analysis for the algorithm's behavior on the sequences s_i).

The paper is logically organized, builds incrementally on prior definitions (consistent languages, noisy closure, noisy closure dimension), and each theorem is proven using previously established lemmas in a traceable chain.
The simplification of the existing characterization (replacing the requirement NC_i(C)<∞ for all i with the single condition NC_1(C)<∞) is a clean and useful distillation of prior work.
weaknesses: The connection to real-world LLM noise/robustness, which is used to motivate the paper in the introduction, is extremely thin. The formal model (languages as abstract infinite subsets of a countable universe, idealized adversarial enumerations) is far removed from anything resembling actual noisy training data, hallucination, or generation quality in deployed LLMs; the motivating paragraph citing empirical robustness literature (co-teaching, DivideMix, reweighting) is essentially decorative and not engaged with substantively elsewhere in the paper.

The contribution is narrow and highly incremental: it resolves two specific open questions from a single very recent paper (RR25) within a niche and rapidly-evolving formal framework (language generation in the limit) that currently has essentially no empirical validation or connection to practical generation/learning algorithms. The audience that would find this directly useful is very small and arguably better served by a learning-theory venue (COLT/ALT), where several of the closely related works in this exact sub-area have in fact been published.

Many key definitions, lemmas, and proof techniques are directly inherited or only mildly adapted from prior work (e.g., Lemma 3.1 is stated as "implicitly contained in [RR25]"), and the paper is essentially a sequence of technical lemmas stacked to answer two specific questions, offering limited new conceptual insight into noise in generation beyond formal bookkeeping.

The paper has no empirical component, and more importantly, no discussion of whether or how the theoretical model's predictions might be tested, validated, or shown relevant to actual language generation systems. The significance of these results to the stated application domain (quantifying the effect of noisy training data on LLMs) remains purely speculative.

The exposition assumes substantial familiarity with at least three prior papers (LRT25, RR25, BPZ26) and their specific notational apparatus (noisy closure, closure dimension, consistent languages), making the paper difficult to assess or appreciate as a standalone piece; a reader unfamiliar with this specific line of work would struggle to evaluate the novelty or importance of the results.

The separation result (Theorem 2.15) and some of the auxiliary machinery (e.g., Lemma 3.2's square-root relationship between NC_{i-1} and NC_i) are presented without much intuition for why these particular combinatorial quantities and bounds are the 'right' ones, reducing the paper's broader pedagogical or methodological value beyond the specific results proven.

No discussion of limitations of the framework itself (e.g., the artificiality of the noise model, countability assumptions, the restriction to a single universe of discrete strings) is provided in the closing remarks, which are quite brief and mostly reiterate the abstract.

strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly stated open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether non-uniform generation is equivalent to non-uniform noise-dependent generation (answered negatively, with a strong separation holding already at noise level 1), and (2) a full characterization of non-uniform noise-dependently generatable collections, which RR25 had conjectured might require conditions beyond the known necessary/sufficient ones.

The central equivalence result (noise level 1 generation is equivalent to any finite noise level i for both uniform and non-uniform generation) is non-obvious and interestingly contrasts with the strict noise-level hierarchy shown for generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026), highlighting a genuine structural difference between the uniform/non-uniform and in-the-limit notions.

The technical machinery (noisy closure dimension, the square-root relation between NC_{i-1} and NC_i in Lemma 3.2, and the careful combinatorial adversary construction in Theorem 2.15) is nontrivial and appears carefully executed; proofs are given in detail and are largely self-contained, aiding verifiability.

The resulting characterization (NC_1(C) < ∞ for uniform noise-dependent generatability) is a meaningful simplification over the prior characterization requiring NC_i(C) < ∞ for every i, which is a clean and useful byproduct of the main technical results.
The paper is well situated within a very active and recently topical line of work (KM24, LRT25, RR25, BPZ26, CP25a/b, etc.), and clearly delineates its contribution relative to this literature.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical/combinatorial with no empirical validation or discussion connecting the formal results back to actual LLM behavior; the motivating claims in the introduction about noisy training data affecting LLMs are only loosely connected to the abstract combinatorial game studied, and the significance of the results for practical language generation/LLM training is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The contribution is narrow and incremental in scope, extending a specific recent sequence of papers (KM24 → LRT25 → RR25 → BPZ26) with proofs that, while nontrivial, are largely technical refinements of existing machinery (noisy closure, consistency) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts or proof techniques.

The construction in the proof of Theorem 2.15 (the key separation result) is intricate and relies on a case analysis (infinitely many indices with f(G(s'_i)) in s_i, vs. not, vs. further sub-cases via Algorithm 1) that is correct-looking but dense; a reader would need to invest significant effort to fully verify correctness, and no intuition-building example or diagram is given to aid understanding of why the construction works.

No discussion of limitations of the framework itself (e.g., how restrictive the noisy-enumeration model is, whether results depend on the specific universe/countability assumptions, or potential implications for more realistic noise models) is included in the closing remarks, despite this being a reasonable place to reflect on scope.

The significance of the work to the broader ICML audience is unclear, as the paper is addressed to a small, highly specialized theoretical subcommunity; the practical implications for designing or understanding real generation/noise-robust algorithms are not discussed beyond a brief motivating paragraph.

strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly stated open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether a single noisy string can strictly reduce generatability (answered affirmatively via Theorem 2.17), and (2) providing a complete characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability (Theorem 2.19/4.7), which RR25 conjectured might require conditions beyond their sufficient/necessary criteria.

The central technical result (Theorem 2.16, that noise level i ≥ 1 is equivalent to noise level 1 for uniform/non-uniform generation) is genuinely surprising given the contrasting strict hierarchy shown by Bai-Panigrahi-Zhang for generation in the limit without the uniform/non-uniform refinement; this juxtaposition is a nice conceptual contribution showing how the uniform/non-uniform lens qualitatively changes the noise landscape.

The proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained, building carefully on machinery (noisy closure, noisy closure dimension) introduced in prior work, with explicit lemma-by-lemma derivations (e.g., Lemma 3.2's counting argument bounding NC_{i-1} in terms of NC_i) rather than hand-waved sketches.

The resulting characterizations (NC_1(C) < ∞ for uniform noise-dependent generation; a countable increasing union condition with NC_1 finiteness for non-uniform) are simpler and more usable than the original per-noise-level characterizations in RR25, which required checking infinitely many conditions.
The related work section is thorough and situates the contribution clearly within a fast-moving subfield, aiding reproducibility of context even though this is a purely theoretical paper.
weaknesses: The contribution is highly specialized to a narrow and fairly young theoretical subfield (formal language generation in the limit with noise variants); the significance for the broader ICML audience is limited, and the paper does not attempt to connect its stylized combinatorial results back to practical LLM training/hallucination phenomena beyond a brief gesture in the introduction.

The Closing Remarks section is only a few sentences and offers essentially no discussion of limitations, broader implications, or promising directions beyond a generic statement hoping to 'spur future exploration'; there is no discussion of what practical insight (if any) the noise-level-1-suffices result offers for real generative systems.

Some of the combinatorial proofs (e.g., the construction in Theorem 2.17 via Algorithm 1, and the partitioning argument in Lemma 3.2) are intricate and dense, making independent verification by a reader difficult without very careful line-by-line checking; the presentation could benefit from more intuition/high-level proof sketches before diving into the formal argument.

The paper is entirely self-contained theory with no illustrative examples of collections C that instantiate the key phenomena (e.g., no example, however small, is given for Theorem 2.16's equivalence result to build reader intuition, only for the separation in Theorem 2.17), which somewhat hampers accessibility even for a theoretically inclined reader.

The abstract sentence 'Finally, we leverage results to provide the first known characterization' appears to have a typo/missing word ('our results' or similar), suggesting the manuscript could use another proofreading pass.

strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly stated open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether non-uniform generation is equivalent to non-uniform noise-dependent generation (answered negatively via Theorem 2.17), and (2) a complete characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability (Theorem 2.19/4.7), which RR25 had conjectured would require conditions beyond their given necessary/sufficient conditions.

The central technical result (Theorem 2.16/3.3/4.2) -- that noise levels i>=1 all collapse to an equivalence class for uniform and non-uniform generation -- is a genuinely surprising and non-trivial finding, especially in contrast with the strict noise-level hierarchy shown for generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026). The contrast is a nice conceptual contribution to the growing literature on noisy generation.

The proofs are detailed, self-contained, and appear mathematically careful (e.g., Lemma 3.2's square-root scaling argument for the noisy closure dimension across noise levels, and the elaborate 'column' construction and case analysis in the proof of Theorem 2.17).

The paper derives a strictly simpler characterization of uniform noise-dependent generatability (NC1(C) < ∞) compared to the previously known characterization requiring NCi(C) < ∞ for all i, which is a clean simplification with explanatory value.
weaknesses: Significance for a broad ICML audience is questionable. The contribution is a narrow, incremental extension within a fast-moving and increasingly crowded sub-niche (language generation in the limit), as evidenced by the extremely long list of near-simultaneous related papers (many dated 2025-2026, several 'to appear' at the same venue). The marginal technical contribution of this paper relative to RR25 and BPZ26 is real but modest, and the paper reads as one incremental step in a sequence of closely related combinatorial results rather than a new conceptual framework or broadly useful tool.

The connection to actual large language models is almost entirely rhetorical. The introduction motivates the work via noisy training data and LLM hallucination, but the formal model (Gold-style enumeration games with adversarially inserted strings) has no empirical grounding or demonstrated relevance to real generation systems; this gap is not discussed as a limitation anywhere in the paper.

No experiments, simulations, or illustrative empirical examples are provided to build intuition for non-expert readers; the entire submission is a dense sequence of definitions, lemmas, and proofs with minimal high-level exposition connecting the results to practical implications.

The presentation assumes very close familiarity with the predecessor papers' notation and definitions (noisy closure, consistency sets, noisy closure dimension, etc. are all imported essentially unchanged from RR25), making the paper difficult to assess or appreciate without reading at least two prior papers in detail; limited original exposition is given to make the paper self-sufficient.

There is no explicit limitations section or discussion of the scope/applicability of the theoretical framework, nor any discussion of broader impact despite the paper explicitly motivating itself via real-world LLM hallucination/noise concerns.

The proof of Theorem 2.17 (the key separation result) is long, case-heavy, and somewhat difficult to verify at a glance (multiple nested cases, an iterative greedy construction via Algorithm 1), raising reproducibility/verifiability concerns for reviewers without substantial dedicated effort.

strengths: The paper resolves two explicitly stated open questions from Raman and Raman (2025): (1) whether non-uniform generation is equivalent to non-uniform noise-dependent generation (answered negatively, with a strong single-noisy-string separation), and (2) a complete characterization for non-uniform noise-dependent generatability.

The central technical result (Theorem 2.16/3.3/4.2) showing that noise levels i≥1 are all equivalent for uniform and non-uniform generation is a genuinely surprising and conceptually interesting finding, especially given its sharp contrast with the strict noise-level hierarchy established by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (2026) for generation in the limit. This contrast is well-motivated and clearly explained.

The key technical lemma (Lemma 3.2) establishing the relation NC_{i-1}(C) ≥ ⌊√(NC_i(C))⌋ is a clever and non-trivial combinatorial argument (via partitioning and closure arguments) that forms the crux of the main collapse result; the proof is carefully structured with clear case analysis.

The resulting characterization (NC_1(C) < ∞) is a meaningful simplification over the prior characterization (which required checking NC_i(C) < ∞ for every i), which is useful for practitioners/theorists applying these criteria.
The paper is well situated in a large and currently very active line of literature, with a thorough related work section situating the contribution relative to many concurrent/recent papers.

The explicit separating construction (Theorem 2.17) is a carefully built, non-trivial combinatorial construction (columns/Bc sets) with a rigorous and exhaustive case analysis (Algorithm 1) showing why no algorithm can non-uniformly generate under even a single unit of noise.
weaknesses: Significance to practical language generation/LLM training is tenuous: the connection drawn in the introduction between this abstract combinatorial game and real noisy training data is largely rhetorical/analogical rather than substantiated, and the paper does not discuss how (if at all) these results might inform practical understanding of noise-robustness in LLMs beyond the toy formal model.

The contribution is a fairly narrow, purely theoretical extension within an already very specific sub-literature (language generation in the limit with noise); while technically interesting, the breadth of impact is limited to a small community of researchers working in this exact framework.

The abstract contains an apparent error/omission: "Finally, we leverage results to provide the first known characterization..." is missing a reference to which results are being leveraged, suggesting insufficient proofreading.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy with limited high-level intuition accompanying several of the more intricate proofs (e.g., Lemma 3.2's construction of partitions and closures), which may significantly hinder accessibility for readers not already deeply familiar with the RR25/BPZ26 framework and definitions.

The paper's novelty is partly incremental in the sense that it operates squarely within the definitional framework and proof techniques (noisy closure, noisy closure dimension) already introduced by Raman and Raman (2025); while the specific collapse result is new and non-obvious, many of the supporting lemmas (e.g., Lemma 3.1, Lemma 4.1) are described as using "standard techniques" or being 'implicitly contained' in prior work, somewhat limiting the sense of methodological originality.

No discussion of limitations of the model itself (e.g., unbounded/adversarial noise insertion positions, the assumption of unique strings, or how sensitive the characterizations are to alternative countable/uncountable universe assumptions) is provided, despite this being a reasonable and low-cost addition for a theory paper.
